15422.description:
## 4-4 Point

AKA star point; hoshi. The 4-4 point allows a player to establish a foothold in a corner while also enabling development of influence. 

Although the 4-4 point favors influence, it is not necessarily inefficient at securing territory. Players should be flexible with this move, ready to adjust their strategy to changing circumstances, at times using it to build influence, at other times going for territory. (p. 10.)

15467.description:

15643.description:
##3-3 Point Invasion

23598.description:
##Shoulder Hit
In the past, this was an unusual play, rarely seen, especially early in the game. It doesn't seem urgent and it isn't sente, but the perception changed when AlphaGo often played it. The idea is to compress Black's position without directly invading. As opposed to an invasion, this play lowers risk and offers a trade of the corner for outside influence. This also fits with the fundamental principle of Go that you don't try to destroy your opponent and get everything, but simply to play better than the opponent so as to get a little more.

Playing a pincer against this shoulder hit is an AI idea that is commonly played. <D:Q9>, <E:R10>, <F:Q10>, and <G:R11> are fixtures in current(2019) professional play but have not quite settled into set patterns yet.

24140.description:
## 3-4 Point

AKA komoku. The 3-4 point favors territory. In this regard, its efficiency is between that of the star and the 3-3 point. Its effectiveness is maximized when the focus is on the corner. Since the 3-4 point is often considered to be the best play for a steady approach to the game, the 3-4 point has been favored by professionals (and AI) over the years. Even so, it lacks the star point's potential for influence and rapid center development. (pp. 6; see also Ishigure Ikuro—In the Beginning, p. 11.)

24146.description:

This approach can also simplify the position, as it generates fewer conventional joseki compared to the more usual approaches. See [Yilun Yang, *2016 Cotsen Open - Yang Yilun 7p vs Liao Guiyong 9p exhibition commentary*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WYO7puzZnrA&t=259s).

The first steps in the opening emphasize the corners. When you play a 3-4 stone, in particular, you should waste no time enclosing the corner. This will usually build about ten points of secure territory.

The value of an enclosure isn't just the points of territory it surrounds. Securing a solid base in the corner makes it easy to develop along either side from the corner.

A corner enclosure generally takes priority over a side extension.

## Small Knight Enclosure
This enclosure is the safest among the four enclosures. The enclosure stone is in the right position to defend against White stepping into the corner at <X:N17>, but has less influence over the right side. This illustrates the basic difference between playing on the third and fourth lines. (p. 10.)

30589.description:
##Shoulder Hit
This move is a weakness of the small knight enclosure. It compresses Black's position without directly invading. As opposed to an invasion, this play lowers risk and offers a trade of the corner for outside influence. It also fits with the fundamental principle of Go that you don't try to destroy your opponent and get everything, but simply to play better than the opponent so as to get a little more.

31230.description:
## 3-3 Point

AKA san san. A 3-3 stone takes the corner completely in one move, although it is low and has diminished mobility. It is most often used by players who are territorially oriented and prepared for long drawn-out battles. It is often used by White. (p. 7.) 

There's no the rush to play an enclosure or approach as with a stone on the 3-4 point. Rather, both players can bide their time until developments elsewhere make an approach or enclosure appropriate. (Ishigure Ikuro—In the Beginning, pp. 12-13.)

[Explanation by Go Magic on Youtube (DDK/SDK)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bygeyuDq5Wk)

[Explanation by Takumi Go Academy on Youtube (SDK/Dan)](https://youtu.be/poHJsj3cp4I?si=Z0vlkbn76P7tZsbE)

31231.description:
##Shoulder Hit

This is the traditional answer to the 3-3 point. 

The direction of Black's next move depends on the positions on the sides.

Crawling once may be the premise for a follow-up move of sliding with a knight's move in the opposite direction. If Black plays at 1 (to the right), the follow-up knight's move is then played at the top. Black's knight's move reduces territory potential on the side it is played. 

Given a White stone on the side, White's move would be a mistake. In such a case, White should have played an extension from that stone, rather than at Q16.

joseki_source.description: Kageyama - Lessons in the Fundamentals of Go

31371.description: <A:Q14> is the only 3-3 enclosure that is played regularly.

31394.description:
## 3-5 Point

AKA mokuhazushi. The 3-5 point is not a common opening play. It emphasizes influence and the side. Since it can often support taking a high position, it has more advantages when fighting globally. So it is more suitable to those who prefer a fighting game. (p. 9.)

Its asymmetrical stance invites an early follow-up play—either an enclosure by Black or an approach by White—as did a stone on the 3-4 point. (Ishigure Ikuro—In the Beginning, p. 16.)

31748.description:
## Joseki

This is the famous Great Slope Joseki (aka Taisha). Once attractive and complicated, it has now been reduced and simplified because of AI. (See [Jiang Weijie, commenting a Samsung Cup game: Shin Jinseo v. Xie Erhao](https://gochn2en.net/wp/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Sumsang_cup_Shin_Xie.pdf).)

White may play at <B:P16> or **Tenuki** to avoid complications. These are compromise moves, so slight disadvantages are inevitable. There are compromise moves even after attaching at <A:Q15>.

<C:O17> and <D:P17> are old joseki and are simpler than the current moves.
